title: At last: A definition of learning
author: Martin Skelton
summary: After thirty-four posts of groundwork, Skelton sets out his working definition: learning is getting better through repeated experiences and good struggle that create, complicate or hardwire neuronal chains, yielding knowledge, skills and understanding over different timescales. He calls it a temporary fixed position, defensible against the evidence he has reviewed but open to amendment. He argues that the value of a definition lies in agreement, drawing on a colleague's distinction between consensus and consent so that a school needs only willingness to go along together. He explains four uses: it can be recognised in classrooms, it can anchor teachers' job descriptions, it helps parents, and it gives students a language for reflecting on their own learning. He offers practical advice to introduce it in small steps rather than as an all-at-once initiative.
points: The definition is defensible because each part derives from the evidence examined earlier, and it is offered as a temporary fixed position rather than the final word.
Schools should aim for consent, not consensus, on what learning means, because a willingness to go along together is attainable where full agreement is not.
The definition translates into a job description for teachers: provide repeated experiences, support good struggle, minimise no struggle and eliminate bad struggle.
Students in schools that share the definition describe their work in terms of consolidating or beginning a skill rather than naming the activity, building metacognition.
Introduce the definition in small steps, since the path to absolutely right is a series of approximately rights.
quotes: I want to stress that this is a definition of learning and not the definition. There are others.

Learning, getting better, happens successfully when our brains, through repeated experiences, engage in a good struggle to a) create or extend an existing neuronal chain b) make a neuronal constellation more complex or c) hardwire an existing chain so that it fires automatically and becomes sticky. When this happens we acquire knowledge, develop our skills and deepen our understandings in different ways and over different periods of time.

Some time ago, one of my colleagues, Pam Harper, coined the phrase for us and it proved to be enduringly useful. We were conscious that a) everything changes over time but that b) we also need to simultaneously think of things as having a fixed quality.

Third, this definition, amended slightly, can be at the heart of a description of what we want teachers to do in classrooms; a part of their job description. We want teachers to provide appropriate repeated experiences, to enable and positively support good struggling, to minimise no struggling and to eliminate bad struggling.

We want teachers to provide appropriate repeated experiences, to enable and positively support good struggling, to minimise no struggling and to eliminate bad struggling. We want teachers to be able, at appropriate times, to tell students factual information, to coach students to become better at their skills and to create opportunities for reflection that enable personal meanings to develop.

In some schools, though, where the students and children share their school’s definition about learning, they give me a different answer. They say, ‘I’m doing this math work to consolidate the learning I have been doing over the past two weeks before we move onto something new’ or ‘Annotating maps is a new skill for us and I am at Beginning level right now.
